speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The panel spent many months last year consulting the public on ways in which pedestrians, cyclists and users of personal mobility devices (PMDs) can safely share public paths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They proposed a set of rules and code of conduct that strike a good balance between the diverse needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Cycling and PMDs have become more popular, not just with the young and active, but even among older Singaporeans as it improves their ability to get around.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is a positive development, as active mobility is a key pillar of our vision for transport in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Cycling and the use of PMDs are convenient and efficient ways of covering short distances, including first- and last- mile connections to bus interchanges or mass rapid transit (MRT) stations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They are essential to Singapore's transition to car-lite mobility, centred on public transport.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Cycling is also emissions-free and contributes to a cleaner and healthier living environment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But with the increasing popularity of bicycles and PMDs, some members of the public have understandably expressed concerns about the safety of pedestrians.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Over the past year, several Members of the House have also asked thoughtful questions and raised helpful suggestions on this issue.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There is not a shadow of doubt that pedestrian safety is paramount.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The panel made it clear that active mobility must be supported by a culture of graciousness and consideration for the safety of others.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The experience of many cities, such as Copenhagen, Amsterdam and Tokyo, attests to this; and our aspiration must be to develop a similar culture of graciousness and consideration for everyone who shares the use of public paths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are still some distance away from attaining the desirable level of graciousness and consideration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: More regularly than we would like, we hear feedback about recklessness by cyclists and PMD users.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As it stands today, I am afraid the burden lies more with cyclists and PMD users to demonstrate that the vast majority of them can be relied upon to be safety-conscious and responsible users of public paths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I am glad that there is a growing fraternity within this group that is determined to do so.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, as with all cultural norms, I am realistic that it may take several years before we get to a new balance, where the different users of public paths can happily co-exist with one another.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our approach must, therefore, take this into account.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We should not ban bicycles and PMDs on footpaths because of the benefits they bring, but we must also act to reduce friction among the different users.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Therefore, we will continue to build more dedicated cycling paths where possible and, at the same time, establish a set of rules and norms for cyclists and PMD users when sharing footpaths with pedestrians.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the same time, to shape a new culture of graciousness, we will need to educate and enforce actively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With this context, let me elaborate on the key provisions in the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, the Bill will set out clearly where bicycles, PMDs and power-assisted bicycles (PABs) can be used.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clauses 6 to 8 empower LTA to define and declare what constitutes a public path where the provisions of this Bill will apply.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In general, all paths in Singapore will be covered by the Bill, except private land, restricted areas, such as military camps and Jurong Island, and areas where access is ticketed, such as the Singapore Zoo and Sentosa.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The use of bicycles, PMDs and PABs in these areas will continue to be regulated by their respective landowners or managers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clauses 15 to 18 outline the types of devices that are permitted on public paths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The first category of public paths are "footpaths".

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: PABs will, however, not be allowed on footpaths, as they pose a greater danger to pedestrians.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The second category of public paths includes today's dedicated and shared cycling paths, and park connectors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These are collectively defined as "shared paths" under the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These shared paths will be clearly demarcated by signs and markings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The third category of paths are "pedestrian-only paths".

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This refers to paths which are not suitable for cycling nor the use of PMDs and PABs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Examples include elevated bridges with low railing heights or steep ramps, such as pedestrian overhead bridges.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will be made clear through "No Riding" signs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These are the key rules to regulate the types of devices allowed on public paths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In addition, the regulations will specify the criteria for bicycles and PMDs that are permitted for use on public paths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They must not weigh more than 20 kilogrammes (kg), be wider than 70 centimetres (cm), or have a maximum device speed exceeding 25 km/h, to be considered compliant.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: PABs are already required to satisfy a more detailed set of requirements under the Road Traffic Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Next, the Active Mobility Bill will allow LTA to apply more stringent penalties for cyclists and users of PMDs and PABs who are caught riding in an unsafe or reckless manner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These penalties will be in addition to the existing penalty under the Penal Code for causing hurt to others by a rash act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will also regulate the sale of devices and take stronger enforcement action against sellers of non-compliant devices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clauses 30 and 32, together with related amendments to the Road Traffic Act, ban the display and advertisement of non-compliant devices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 34 prohibits the sale of non-compliant devices for use on public paths, while clause 35 makes it an offence to modify devices in a manner that makes them non-compliant.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Sellers found displaying or advertising a non-compliant PMD will be liable upon conviction to a fine not exceeding $1,000, or to imprisonment not exceeding three months, or both.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Those found selling non-compliant devices or illegally modifying PMDs will be liable upon conviction to a fine not exceeding $5,000, or to imprisonment not exceeding three months, or both.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Bill will grant LTA stronger and more expansive enforcement powers, for better deterrence and enforcement against errant users and sellers of non-compliant devices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: LTA has already been deploying Active Mobility Enforcement Officers to educate the public on the rules and norms in the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When the Bill is passed, LTA officers will be able to also issue notices of offence to, and prosecute offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To improve the effectiveness of enforcement, clause 44 will allow LTA enforcement officers to enter and inspect businesses suspected of committing offences, such as illegally modifying devices and selling non-compliant devices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clauses 50 and 51 empower LTA to seize and forfeit non-compliant devices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clauses 45 to 49 will grant LTA enforcement officers other powers to allow them to carry out their duties effectively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These include but are not limited to powers to remove obstructions from public paths; to examine bicycles, PMDs and PABs; to demand information for identification of suspected offenders; and to arrest persons who refuse to cooperate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: LTA's enforcement efforts will be supported by the National Parks Board (NParks) and Traffic Police.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 39 empowers LTA to appoint employees of other public authorities, such as NParks, as public path wardens, who will then have the same powers to carry out enforcement in parks and along park connectors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Education is equally important if we are to build up a culture of safety and graciousness.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: LTA has enlisted the help of Active Mobility Patrol Volunteers from the community and grassroots in this regard.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The volunteers can also serve as useful "eyes" to detect errant behaviour.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Hence, clause 41 grants limited powers to the volunteers, to allow them to obtain personal particulars from suspected offenders, to advise them to stop engaging in offending conduct, and to document evidence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The volunteers will, however, not be given more intrusive powers, such as to inspect, seize and forfeit devices, nor powers of arrest.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 55(2)(b) will empower LTA, with the approval of the Public Prosecutor, to require offenders of compoundable offences to attend LTA's Safe Cycling Programme before they are allowed to compound the offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Offenders who fail to complete the Programme will be charged in Court.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will make a few amendments to related Acts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Every PAB used on public roads and public paths will, henceforth, be required to carry a registration plate and be registered to an owner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In summary, Mdm Speaker, this Bill empowers LTA to regulate the sale and use of bicycles, PMDs and PABs on public paths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It will allow us to safeguard the safety of pedestrians even as we encourage active mobility.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our aim is to shape a culture where there is gracious and considerate sharing of public paths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: While cultural norms take time to develop, we can support their formation through appropriate rules and enforcement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will continue to monitor the situation on the ground and evolve these rules as necessary to promote active mobility in support of a car-lite Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Our Government has worked hard to achieve a sustainable public transportation system that is affordable, convenient and efficient for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Active Mobility, which includes walking, cycling and the use of personal mobility devices (PMDs) will support this system.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There are, however, two questions which I wish to raise.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: One, is the regulation contained in the Active Mobility Bill sufficient to protect the safety and well-being of other pathway users?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It includes regulation which prohibits modifications of PMDs beyond what is allowed by law, speeding offences, dangerous and/or reckless riding offences and also mandates that users of PMDs do not leave the scene in the case of an accident and render assistance.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: To a large degree, these mirror those regulations for motor vehicles codified under the Road Traffic Act.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The question, as I alluded to earlier, is whether more can and should be done to protect the safety and well-being of other pathway users.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: First, unlike drivers of motor vehicles, PMD users will not be licensed.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There is no minimum age requirement for PMD users and they are not required to attain any minimum level of competency before being allowed to operate PMDs.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This means that PMD users in Singapore are likely to vary greatly in terms of maturity and competency levels when operating PMDs.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Second, Singapore is ranked as one of the densest cities in the world.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Our residential towns or suburban areas, which centre around high-rise public housing, accentuates this.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is unlike other cities which may have dense city centres but less dense suburban residential areas.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is also important to note that our dense residential towns are also where more vulnerable classes of Singaporeans, such as the less mobile elderly and young children, are likely to share pathways with PMD users.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Third, the aim of the Active Mobility Bill is to encourage more Singaporeans to consider the use of PMDs as an alternative to driving.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If this vision succeeds, we would expect a significant increase in PMD users on our pathways from the numbers we see now.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Such increased numbers, coupled with varying competency levels of PMD users, raise the risk factors and the likelihood of unfortunate accidents involving PMDs.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Senior Minister of State Josephine Teo had said in her reply to various Parliamentary Questions raised by Members on 10 October 2016 that "the careless behaviour of a small minority of users has caused accidents and led to some members of the public to oppose their (the PMD) proliferation.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It would be unfortunate if we allowed the careless behaviour of this small minority to prevent the larger majority of responsible and considerate cyclists and PMD users from enjoying the benefits of such travel modes".

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I agree with the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I do not suggest that PMDs be banned.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: However, as the situational context is likely to cause the number of unfortunate accidents involving PMDs to rise, I ask if we can do more.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Or at least vary the age limits for different types of PMDs depending on the technical requirements of operation?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Can penalties for recalcitrant or repeat offenders be increased to serve as a deterrent to irresponsible PMD users?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Is it feasible to impose a ban on such recalcitrant or repeat offenders from using PMDs in the future?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: These suggestions are not meant as a criticism of the Active Mobility Bill but an illustration on the possibility of doing more.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As the Bill stands, the proposed regulation is robust and sufficiently addresses our current situational needs.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: However, as the use of PMDs proliferate and our situational needs change, we must ensure that we do more to protect the safety and well-being of responsible and considerate PMD users and pedestrians alike.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Fortunately for Mdm Ang and her family, she has since recovered well enough to return home.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is extremely heart-warming news and I am sure this House will join me in wishing Mdm Ang a full and complete recovery from her injuries.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But Mdm Ang's gradual recovery from her injuries comes with significant financial and medical costs.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In this case, Mdm Ang is a housewife while her husband is the breadwinner for the family.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: What if the accident victim was the sole breadwinner of his or her family?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Financial aid and social welfare can only go so far.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Keeping this in mind, our injury compensation scheme must, therefore, be a robust one that can adequately and fairly compensate accident victims who suffer personal injuries.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: For motor vehicles, we have the Motor Vehicles (Third Party Risks and Compensation) Act.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The Act makes it mandatory for all motor vehicles to have compulsory third-party insurance.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In cases where it is a hit and run or if there is no insurer concerned, where there is no identifiable insurer, the Motor Insurance Bureau (MIB) steps in by arrangement to bridge the gap.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In other words, motor accident victims who suffer personal injury are fully assured of receiving some form of compensation for their personal injuries.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If the intention is to proliferate the use of PMDs in conjunction with the Public Transportation System to reduce our reliance on cars, this will mean that the use of PMDs is likely to increase significantly as more Singaporeans learn and accept the use of PMDs as an alternative mode of transport.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If this happens, our pathways are likely to get more crowded with PMD users and more accidents involving PMDs may happen.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is not something that every individual or family can afford.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Even if a civil suit is won, there are instances where a plaintiff could only obtain a paper judgment when the defendant has no means to pay the sum awarded by the Court.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Further, it is not unforeseeable to surmise that "hit and run" cases involving PMD users could potentially be higher than motor vehicles.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Motor vehicles are large and carry licence plates which can be identified by witnesses of motor accidents.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Irresponsible and reckless PMD users could hit other PMD users or pedestrians and run off before anyone can react.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This could potentially leave us with many unwitting accident victims involving PMDs with no recourse to seek compensation for any personal injury suffered.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This will need further in-depth discussions and consideration, but it is definitely an issue that needs to be urgently addressed as the use of PMDs become more and more prevalent in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A Bill dedicated to ensuring active mobility through the increased use of bicycles, e-scooters and other personal mobility devices is, indeed, timely.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Setting out the regulations on the speed and weight of the vehicles as well as where they can be used have all been addressed quite thoroughly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At the heart of this Bill is the safety of the users and, just as importantly, the pedestrians.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Let us bear in mind that walking and running to a destination are also part of our national drive to promote active mobility while reducing our carbon footprint.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Bill also addresses the conditions for the future development of dedicated travel paths on public and private land, in tandem with the Ministry's intention to create a more conducive landscape for multiple modes of travel and transportation, where walking, jogging, cycling, driving and various forms of public transport complement one another, providing a wide range of alternatives for reaching destinations; all the while encouraging healthy active lifestyles.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Unlike cars, PMDs do not have identifiable numbers or tags and if the culprits are determined to evade responsibilities, it would be very difficult to identify them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that the Ministry will continue to think of ways to ensure that such devices are easily identified and visibly tagged.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Currently, the idea of licensing and even tagging them with mini-In-Vehicle-Units, like for cars, have been rejected based on the reason that it is costly and not practical.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, without doing so, in reality, it would be very difficult to apprehend the culprits.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some are afraid that there could be fraud such as the use of fake licensing tags.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, in fact, vehicles also face the same problem.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is not so difficult to change the licensing plate of a vehicle.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will ensure that victims can at least be assured of compensation in the event of injury or death, encouraging the users to report the accidents as well.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With increased usage, the number of accidents will increase.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, I urge the Ministry to consider improving road and pathway design to protect all users better, separating riders from pedestrians wherever possible, as we go forward to ensure greater safety for all.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This has already been done in certain segments of New York City.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The design can be done in such a way that discourages mobility devices from encroaching upon the space for pedestrians.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Walkways could be slightly raised and made a little uneven, such that it poses little difference to pedestrians but is bumpy for those on riding devices.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Lastly, I hope the Ministry would consider providing community volunteers with light, wearable video equipment to make it easier for them to carry out their jobs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This would be helpful for them as they are on the ground daily and can nip any problem in the bud earlier and faster.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the recent fatal accidents involving motor vehicles and users of e-scooters and power-assisted bicycles, it is crucial to put in place legislative guidelines to better govern the usage of these new transportation devices.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As more favour the use of such PMDs and PABs to get to their destinations, there is a pressing need for the authorities to adopt a firm approach to create a safe and responsible active mobility culture in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even with legislation, other road users will also need to be more vigilant to safeguard their personal safety and to look out for others.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Like many members of the public, I am concerned about the safety of pedestrians who share their paths with PMD users.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will there be an increase in the number of enforcement officers deployed island-wide and over a sustained period?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There is a current ban on PABs on park connectors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the speed limit of electric (e)-bikes capped at 25 km/h, I would like to seek clarification from the Minister if this would mean that these LTA-compliant e-bikes will be allowed on park connectors, so that it is easier for riders to get from point A to point B, as compared to riding on the roads?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If this is so, I would like to suggest then for NParks and LTA to explore ways to better monitor the park connectors, such as through the installation of CCTV cameras.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Footages from these CCTVs can help facilitate investigations in the event of an accident.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This would also serve to safeguard the interests of all park users.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Faced with land constraints, particularly in mature estates, it would be a challenge to carve out shared paths to accommodate both pedestrians and users of PMDs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is essential that shared paths are neither too narrow nor too steep to ensure safety and ample space for every user.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have spoken about the need to protect pedestrians.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There is also a need to educate PMD and PAB users on how to keep themselves safe.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is especially important for PAB users who are allowed to ride on public roads.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Other road users, such as car drivers and motorcyclists, need to pass theory and practical tests to gain the necessary safety knowledge before they are allowed on the roads.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We can also do more to ensure the physical safety of PMD and PAB users.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Currently, only cyclists and PAB users are encouraged to wear helmets.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is especially in view of the recent death of 23-year-old Mr Sam Koh who died of a serious head injury after falling off his electric scooter in March last year.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Proper use of a helmet could help mitigate serious head injuries in the event of an accident.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Residents have told me of near misses involving fast moving PMDs on shared paths.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It would be helpful if these PMDs can be made more visible to other path users, particularly in low light conditions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would LTA consider mandatory installation of front and rear lights for all motorised PMDs?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My colleague Mr Sitoh Yih Pin had brought up the same case: in September last year, 53-year-old housewife Madam Ang Liu Kiow was hit by an electric scooter.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would also like to propose that the Bill expands its legislative powers to make it an offence for an online retailer to sell non-compliant devices.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Currently, the Bill makes it an offence for a retailer to sell or display non-compliant personal mobility devices within a shop's premises.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, the Bill makes no specific mention of online retailers, which are a popular point-of-sale for such non-compliant devices.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would also like to urge the Ministry to consider mandating the installation of registration plates on all PABs as this can act as a prominent identifier to help enforcement officers identify the PAB and facilitate tracing of the PAB owner in the event of an accident.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Also, are there any lessons from the National Environment Agency's (NEA's) Community Volunteer Programme which can be useful to improve the Active Mobility Patrol Scheme?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What matters most is how an individual behaves when using their PMD or PAB.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Legislation is only a first step towards creating public awareness on what is right and wrong, with legal penalties serving to deter reckless behaviour.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The responsibility of creating safer roads and pathways lies with every individual.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With that, Mdm Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, I would like to touch on three issues relating to cycling and mobility issues in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They are cycling culture, political will and public education.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Cycling has been one of my favourite past times since I was in school.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Having lived near the East Coast Park for years, I spent many happy moments on the cycling paths of East Coast Park.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As the park became more and more crowded on weekends over the years, I have been avoiding cycling in the park itself.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why do I avoid cycling in East Coast Park?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think it has become unsafe over the years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many cyclists do not obey the direction signs or keep a proper lookout for pedestrians or other cyclists.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many pedestrians walk on or across the cycling paths without caring for the safety of cyclists.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have seen accidents in the park over the years, accidents that can be avoided if we had the right cycling culture.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Although most cyclists comply with the law and have good cycling habits, some of the following acts are still carried out by a minority of cyclists on an everyday basis.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When I say "cyclists", I also include electric bikes and PMD users.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And the examples are, when on roads, beating red lights or cycling against the traffic, and when on public paths and park connectors, cycling at high speed, not keeping left and not giving way, thus creating the risk of accident with pedestrians or other users.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When I was at university in England, my second-hand road bike was my main form of transport.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even in those years in the early 1990s, the law required everyone to cycle on the roads, not on footpaths or pavements, and to keep left when cycling.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When it was dark, everyone had to use a standard set of white front lights and red rear lights.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Everyone seemed to follow the law and practice.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the first few weeks at university, I learnt a very important lesson about cycling culture.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I mistakenly got onto a footpath and was roundly told off by an elderly lady.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Everybody knows what to expect about cycling and cyclists.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A pedestrian will not expect to meet a cyclist coming his way except when dismounted.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A motorist will not expect to see a cyclist cycling against the traffic.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is certainty and, importantly, this breeds mutual respect among all users and I believe that that, in turn, promotes a better and safer environment for cyclists and cycling and road users.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is important for Singapore because cycling is not going to go away or bicycles banned from the roads, and e-scooters, PMDs and e-bikes are all here to stay.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has talked about bicycles being an important element for the final-mile connectivity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Having a safe and good cycling culture will definitely promote that.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Around 10 years ago, I remember there was at one time a flurry of complaints in the newspapers about non-enforcement against errant cyclists.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Cyclists cycling on the wrong side of the road or beating red lights were already common occurrences then.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I remember once when the authorities replied to say that they had inadequate resources to address the problem.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lack of resources might well be the given reason but it looked to me that this issue was not a priority then and there was no will to deal with the problems at that time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the effect is that the can is kicked down the road.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We missed a great opportunity to solve the problem back then in the mid-2000s.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In those days, the only people who seemed to have broken the law were elderly cyclists.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But after that, there was a huge influx of foreign workers and this meant a huge increase in the number of people using bicycles and many also followed the cycling culture: ignoring the road safety rules because of lax enforcement.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And then from the late 2000s, with the increase in white collar foreign labour, we also saw many of them taking up recreational road cycling at the same time as many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the number of bicycles on the road have continued to increase in the last 10 over years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many people who use them regard them as a cheap and unlicensed substitute for scooters and motorcycles.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And finally, we have e-scooters or PMDs in the last two to three years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have been hearing of accidents involving PABs for a while and, lately, accidents involving e-scooters.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think it is now harder to improve our cycling culture.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I know LTA is now trying harder to carry out enforcement actions and putting out regular advisories or publicity about their actions on their Facebook page.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: LTA also has volunteers to do the messaging for the new cycling rules.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I really appreciate all that and hope that we are finally moving in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I can imagine the authorities will need a lot of resources.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But when will the day come when we do not see the acts that I talked about on a daily or regular basis?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What are the Government's plans to ensure that members of the public will be able to adapt to the new signages without any confusion?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I can imagine that there will be much public education required.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On this note, let me talk about public education.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For many years, the Government has been talking about having public education on safety in cycling.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This Bill may still be inadequate without regular and strict enforcement, together with effective public education.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is particularly important if we are not going to be able to require compulsory third-party insurance for bicycles, e-bikes and PMD users.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Go to any public park during the weekends, and we can see many children using bicycles and skate scooters.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is important that we engender in our young children the culture of safe and considerate riding when they start riding.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government should consider having appropriate lessons on cycling culture and road safety.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also mentioned that throttle may be more suitable for some users as they do not need some strength to pedal and "kick in" the electric power required in current authorised models.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And if throttle is a no-no for e-bikes because of safety issues, how does the Government reconcile that with its position on e-scooters?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have seen many e-scooters going at high speeds on the roads and get into accidents on the road or on footpaths.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have read from media reports that some had a speed as high as 80 km/h.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Speaker, I support this Bill.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government encourages more people to use bicycles and other PMDs in order to build a car-lite society and offer Singaporeans more mobility choices.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, we need to create a good environment for walking and have suitable facilities.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, the designated bicycle lanes in Ang Mo Kio, the redesigned wider lanes along Bencoolen Road, and additional bicycle parking facilities, will make things easier and safer for pedestrians and PMD users.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More importantly, pedestrians, PMD users and drivers need to have the right mindset in terms of sharing the road with one another.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have four suggestions for the Ministry of Transport's (MOT's) consideration.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, the operators need to be more responsible.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The importers should not only import up-to-standard PMDs, but also introduce PMDs with more safety features.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The retailers should also proactively teach their customers how to use PMDs properly.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They can consider collaborating with certain groups to teach buyers how to use their PMDs safely.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They can consider recording or taking photos of the repair work details.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: MOT can also recommend repair companies that uphold a high safety standard to people who require repair services.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, the scope of enforcement should also be more comprehensive.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The design and speed limits of some roads in industrial zones and highways may not be suitable for co-use by bicycles or PABs.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can we tighten rules with regard to the usage of these roads?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Perhaps we can put up more noticeable signs or ban bicycles or PABs from using these roads?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have seen a mother taking her child to school on a PMD.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although it is convenient, we should not allow it because of safety reasons.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If possible, we should have rules, such as only one passenger is allowed and that both should also wear appropriate protective gear, like a helmet.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Third, we should have appropriate facilities for PMDs.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To encourage more people to use public transport and PMDs, we must improve our road design, display appropriate signs or create designated lanes for PMDs.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Earlier, some Members mentioned that, when it comes to road design, we can have traffic calming measures, such as narrowing the road and creating roundabouts, to limit car speed and improve road safety.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Perhaps, for the next stage, we can consider setting up designated MRT cars for people to board and alight the train.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This way, they will not affect other passengers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have seen some coffeeshops providing charging facilities for customers to charge their devices.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am also glad to see new MRT stations having more bicycle and PAB parking facilities.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: LTA is also gradually expanding the parking facilities at existing MRT stations.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Now, there are more people who go out on bicycles or PMDs to work, school or shopping malls.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some of my residents use their PMDs to go to the community centre (CC) to exercise or attend classes.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, it is not convenient for them to bring these devices into their classroom and they cannot leave their PMDs outside with peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I will have some transparent storage cabinets installed at Cheng San Community Centre and increase bicycle parking spaces.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will make it more convenient for my residents.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In order to have more such facilities, we need facilitation from MOT.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If MOT can help shopping malls and other places to convert some parking spaces into parking storage facilities for bicycles, PABs and PMDs, it will make things more convenient for their users.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The fourth and the last suggestion is to increase safety awareness.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are all very familiar with the Highway Code.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Code is akin to a road usage guideline, listing down the proper behaviour of a road user to prevent accidents from happening.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As PMD users increase, we not only need to educate drivers of the importance of safe driving, we must also pay attention to PMD users.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Similarly, the Government can also consider amending the teaching materials and include important information with regard to PMDs into the Highway Code, thus improving drivers' safety awareness of PMD users.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This can increase our overall sense of safety.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ultimately, I hope to see that every pedestrian, every PMD user and every driver is willing to share our limited space by being considerate and courteous to others, as well as abiding by the rules.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On top of that, if we also have appropriate facilities, then our travelling speed may become slower, but accidents will become less, and everyone's journey will be more pleasant and convenient.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Clause 3 of the Bill clearly identifies the aims of the new Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The basic reason why this issue arises at all is because we are a space-constrained country.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Limited space must be shared, but the rules for sharing cannot be assumed to always be known.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Unlike motor vehicle usage on roadways, sharing of active mobility devices is not as natural as it appears because it depends on factors about a range of usage patterns and pathway conditions that are actually much more varied than on roads.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: One key issue in this matter is user behaviour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Would this not endanger both the users of PMDs, bicycles and PABs who do this, as well as motor vehicles which unexpectedly encounter them?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Another clause that I want to ask about is clause 16(2), which refers explicitly to footpaths.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: What I would like to ask the Senior Minister of State is whether she could clarify if it applies to the following related situations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: When cyclists and PMD users switch between pedestrian walkways and roadways, their actions become unpredictable to other users.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This lack of predictability ends up increasing the danger to everyone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Cyclists and PMD users also stray into bus lanes during restricted hours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The speeds of various users vary greatly on our roads and our pathways and are much less subject to regulation when they are on shared pathways.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: A young child riding a bicycle is very different from an adult speeding and expecting others to give way to him.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Older pedestrians who experience issues with mobility often feel a need to get out into the open and move around, but those of us who have older dependants know that we worry more about them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Do we have to worry now about their safety in the face of the increasingly intense usage by new classes of PMDs?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: If incidents increase and arguments about right of way become more prevalent, will we be seeing a call for more directional signs on pedestrian pathways, such as those used on roads for heavier vehicles?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: A proliferation of signages will only spawn a new set of challenges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Right of way, where pathways intersect with driveways, could lead to increased chances of dispute and accidents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The proposed Bill allows for the appointment of public path wardens, as set out in clause 39.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: A public path warden's role would involve determining whether violations of clauses 15(2)(a), 15(2)(b) and 18(1)(b) have occurred.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: We should already be familiar with the challenges that are likely to be involved in such cases, especially because of the experiences of parking and road traffic wardens.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, judging by the types of situations that traffic wardens could be required to react to, it would not be unreasonable to predict that their roles could be much more challenging and, therefore, that they should require more training.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In addition to making quick decisions about whether the technical specifications of PMBs and PABs are prescribed or banned, a public path warden would also need to have skills in dealing with the public in situations where argumentation is much more likely to arise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Given the expectations of such enforcers, where are we going to get a supply of such skilled personnel?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Will public path wardens also be required to deal with problems arising from inappropriate design of PMDs, such as the effect their headlights have on drivers of other motor vehicles?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The headlights on PMDs could affect the vision of other drivers at night, especially when they travel in opposite directions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: If PMDs end up taking over footpaths, pedestrians will end up getting crowded out.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Will pedestrians, therefore, ultimately, be the ones suffering as a result?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: If there is a conflict between the two, which one should we prioritise ‒ pedestrian comfort or the habits of PMD users?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While the evolution and use of such devices have been rapid, there is no doubt that a set of easily understandable rules needs to be implemented to govern the use of such devices for the safety of all.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While I am supportive of this Bill and its objectives, I seek a few clarifications with regard to some of the clauses of the Bill and will raise them in chronological order.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On clause 2, the intention of using the noun "pedestrian" in the Bill appears to separate fast-moving individuals from those who are slower so that the pedestrian-only path is in some ways protected from bicycles or other vehicles.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But in day-to-day life, this may cause confusion, especially when skateboards are classified as PMDs while people on inline or roller skates are classified as pedestrians.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: People on inline or roller skates can move fairly quickly and potentially cause harm to other pedestrians as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How did the Ministry settle on the definition of who is a pedestrian and who is not?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While this may be a matter of judgement and the Ministry wishes to be unambiguous about the seriousness of such violations or to facilitate uncomplicated interpretation, would not a more incremental legislative approach, starting with fines only, represent a more communicative and educative policy-making exercise so as to allow people to understand the rules more and to allow a passage of time to pass before Parliament determines whether or not to review the sentences, based on ground feedback?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such an incremental approach could also assist to reinforce a safety culture involving PABs and PMDs over time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would it not be administratively more efficient for the relevant authorities, specifically LTA and NParks, for example, to bear the cost of erecting and maintaining signages?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This would also be administratively convenient as there would be a clear standardisation of such signs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If proprietors or occupiers have to purchase signages from officially-approved agents, would it not be better to have the relevant authorities just take charge instead?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would it not be enough for businesses to remind customers about which models are compliant or not before the purchase, which is provided for in the warning notices specified in clause 30?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Anecdotally, the legality of models is a big concern for people looking to buy PMDs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would appear excessive to potentially jail sellers for failing to keep non-compliant PMDs out of the sight of customers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The same concerns are relevant for clause 31, which calls for a fine and/or jail term for advertising non-compliant PMDs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Clause 33 states that a person shall be guilty of an offence if, at the time of sale, "the person knows that or is reckless as to whether or not the buyer intends to ride the PMD on a public road".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If the clause would cover sales at any premises or place so it can be assumed that it would cover private individuals selling their used PMDs on Carousell, for example, how would the Ministry determine whether or not a seller is "reckless" as to the buyer's intentions to ride the PMD on a public road?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is failure to ask the buyer specifically if he or she intends to ride it on a public road considered an offence?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If the buyer says no but rides on the road anyway, is the seller guilty of an offence because he or she did not question the buyer further?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Clause 33 also states that it is not a defence for the accused to prove that warning notices were displayed in accordance with clause 31.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If so, what would constitute a defence, short of a written agreement or an agreement that is captured on video?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How many buyers or sellers would do this?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To conclude, Mdm Speaker, this Bill seeks to govern the behaviour of individuals who use PMDs and PABs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Members would be aware that not just Singaporeans but many foreigners, especially those who live and work near industrial estates, also use such devices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One key challenge would be to educate a large and transient foreign worker community of these norms.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As with any transient group, the effort would have to be a continuous one.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The effectiveness of this legislation on the ground will be directly correlated to the amount of effort that is put in to educate all users, Singaporeans and foreigners alike, of the codes of conduct that can be issued by the Minister under clause 24 of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is not just the Government's role or the Government's job, but, of course, it is the job of all users.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It was heart-wrenching to witness the family's trauma from nearly losing a loved one to an accident which could have been avoided.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe, if you could see the family, then you would understand the rationale and intent of introducing what we are introducing in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Sadly, that was not the last accident involving users of PMD, despite all the public education that was mounted.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I could not imagine the trauma the family must have faced.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Despite these accidents, the reality now is that we will see increasing users of these PMDs.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Modernisation in technology has expanded transport options for commuters and usage of PMDs.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These modes are also rapidly picking up in popularity.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe that it is high time that this Bill was introduced for these commuters who choose to adopt alternative modes of transport, be it for cost-savings, physical disability, convenience or even environmental considerations, to ensure that we create a living space safe for all to use.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Several other countries have successfully implemented active mobility initiatives and there are several good models available for us to adopt and even improve upon.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That said, there are two areas that I would like to address, namely, safety and administration.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While some may prefer the education route to promote mutual understanding among different road users, penalties to errant and irresponsible parties are necessary to enforce the right behaviour.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Second, I also suggest expanding the law to ban the use of bicycles, including e-bicycles, on the main road, to those under 18 years of age.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Younger PMD users must use the shared footpaths or dedicated cycling tracks and must refrain from using the main roads.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Third, while motorists are required to pass their Highway Code, such a requirement does not exist for PMD users who ride on the main road.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Unfamiliarity with road signs among PMD users may increase the risk of them being involved in accidents.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, the Government may want to consider making it compulsory for PMD users to have basic Highway Code knowledge.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Fourth, I would also like the Government to consider raising the penalties for PMD users for riding under the influence of alcohol.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Riding under the influence of alcohol is extremely dangerous not just for the rider, but for fellow motorists and pedestrians as well.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is practised in Japan where PMD users with repeated offences are required to attend a road etiquette course or risk stiff fines.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   Mdm Speaker, I believe it is timely to introduce the Active Mobility Bill.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Despite campaigns and education efforts to promote responsible behaviour among users of PMDs, we are still seeing families losing their loved ones in tragic accidents involving PMD users, especially e-scooters and e-bicycles.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: By having insurance coverage available, it will help ensure that due compensations can be made without significant financial strains to all the parties involved.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, the Active Mobility Bill is a big undertaking, and I am positive that it holds great merit in making Singapore a much more liveable city for everyone.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With proper attitudes and complementary infrastructure, active mobility will be a great boon for our residents who wish to take up these alternative modes of transport to ease them in their daily lives.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Recently, there had been more news and reported cases as awareness was raised about such mobility devices, and the easy access to recording tools have helped some victims gain their much needed justice.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Noting the stiffer penalty meted out in some earlier cases, some people may be cautious.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But it does not allay the fears many would have, especially those who were once the undeserved victims.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As the Ministry continues to fine tune the Act, I support for three areas to be constantly reviewed: (a) education strategies; (b) enforcement; and (c) planning and design of shared spaces.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: On education strategies, studies have shown that human behaviours can be influenced by repeating certain actions and many of the behavioural traits can be changed through mindshare and are more effectively captured at a young age.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I recall in my growing years, we were exposed to many campaigns, from Singa Lion − the Singapore Kindness Movement; Teamy Bee − efficient, productive workforce; to Sharity elephant and so on.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In each campaign, it was not simply the mascot or the songs that we remembered.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It was the inculcating of the key messages and the actions that we undertook in and out of the classes that remained with us as useful values in life.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As part of raising awareness in the education campaign, I support those aspects concerning road safety and use of public shared spaces to be widely broadcasted.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The campaign must be done on multiple fronts, not only in schools, and to be continued for a period of time, especially when there are new rulings in place.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Everyone in the community must eventually have a sense of responsibility in using all the shared spaces and know right from wrong without being told or trolled on social media.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Thus, over time, our behaviours and unwritten rules should reflect the way we can co-exist harmoniously and safely with considerate thoughts for others.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This is a fundamental question when we look at the necessity for more enforcement and also the safety of road users.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Typically, users of these PMDs or bicycles do not have the appropriate protective gears and alarms for signalling or even notifying others when in danger.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Chances of them appearing at risky positions to the vehicles and with little room to manoeuvre are high.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: They will unintentionally end up endangering themselves and the nearby vehicles if they do not know who has the right of way on public roads.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Since clause 3 sets out the purposes of the Bill, one of which is to enhance connectivity by supporting developments that promote walking and cycling and patronage of our public transport, then I would say understanding the road conditions, such as when not to take risks and how to be a better road user, are important knowledge for these users to acquire.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Regulations and enforcement are necessary measures for rules to be upheld and in cases where disputes are most likely to occur between independent parties.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: However, there can never be sufficient ground enforcement if the penalties are not steep to deter the act of an offence or if the location and number of offences are widespread, thus making it hard to capture these offences.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: On this note, I would like to seek a few clarifications from the Minister.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: If the Police investigations do not reveal any new findings or are unable to identify the offender, how can the victims be compensated?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Also, to what extent is the seller required to put up warning notices for an online sale that is in accordance with clause 31?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Four, apart from fines and imprisonment for repeat offenders, would the Ministry consider having the offender contribute a certain number of hours to community service similar to the Corrective Work Order for those who litter?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Five, I understand that some PMDs are designed with speed limit detectors and, as a safety measure, its maximum limit would be capped within the specified range as set out by LTA.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: My question is how can we ensure that the safety limit trigger continues to be functional over time and would LTA consider reducing the speed for paths when the users are travelling in downhill motions?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: On the last area, planning and design of shared spaces.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In many estates and public spaces, we have increasingly seen many bollards and boards being put up to prevent all these fast-moving bicycles and PMDs from knocking into pedestrians.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Not only are they unsightly, they are not completely effective at some junctions and they also pose a challenge for those users who are in wheelchairs or those with baby strollers as they have to move around all these obstacles.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Moving forward, there are more cycling networks planned to be added to connect our housing estates to major traffic nodes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This will undoubtedly provide relief to both cyclists and pedestrians.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: However, the widening of footpaths brings along with it joy and also sorrow.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: So, what more can be done in this area?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This would be most welcomed, especially when it needs to do strict enforcement.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Thus, I hope that some of the suggestions could be looked into and I seek feedback on the clarifications that I have put across.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We also support the various measures proposed to promote and ensure the safety of users of public paths.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This Bill will set out the legal framework and code of conduct for all users of public paths to minimise conflicts among the users and support our nation's drive towards a car-lite society.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: These footpaths, including covered footpaths, are mainly the common property of the Town Councils.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Town Councils are responsible to maintain these footpaths and enforce the by-laws to ensure the safe use of these footpaths.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: These complaints include: (a) speeding and reckless riding, (b) illegal parking of bicycles, and (c) disputes among users of footpaths.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The definitions of pedestrians, riders and various types of footpaths are quite confusing.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: It may be easier for the public to understand if we just classify public paths into walking path, cycling path and walk-and-cycle path.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Walking path shall allow users to walk, move on motorised and non-motorised wheelchairs, ride mobility scooters or PMDs, pull trolleys or skates.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: While cycling paths are for riders using bicycles or PABs.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: To avoid confusion, we need to clearly mark walking and cycling paths with footprints or bicycle prints respectively at regular intervals.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: If not, who will be responsible to maintain and enforce the use of these declared public paths in the town?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Who will take up the public liability insurance for the public paths?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Closed circuit television (CCTV) cameras can be installed at high-risk locations to regulate the use of all public paths.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Mobile CCTVs can also be deployed to facilitate enforcement efforts on reckless riders.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I would propose that LTA set up a 24-hour hotline to follow up on feedback from the users.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In addition, LTA should deploy enforcement teams in every constituency to educate and instil discipline among users of public paths.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: To facilitate enforcement, LTA should consider registering all riders, bicycles and PABs.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: To avoid disputes among users, I would propose that LTA build more dedicated and separate cycling paths connecting to MRT stations, town centres and various amenities in the town.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: By separating walking and cycling paths, both pedestrians and cyclists will enjoy safer use of public paths.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This will enable LTA to gather feedback and understand the concerns of the users.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In this way, more effective measures can be taken to fine-tune the Act in future to promote walking and cycling in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I looked at the effect of high-speed motor cars on human and social psychology.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To borrow the words of an English novelist, JG Ballard, "I think the 20th century reaches its highest expression on the highway.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Everything is there: the speed and violence of our age; the strange love affair with the machine, with its own death." My apologies to start a new year in my speech with such a grim image, but I do think that both walking and cycling would really provide a good antidote to a society that is driven by speed to a point where civility, a lot of times, is ignored and lost.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I think this Bill is a good step towards a cultural shift in our mobility choices by protecting the safety of all users of pathways.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: However, I would like to express my concern on the structural and spatial design of existing and future pathways that might frustrate some of the purposes of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: My concern is that existing pedestrian-only paths and footpaths might not be wide enough to accommodate such usage, thereby leading to accidents.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Second, it is worthwhile to invest in smart, protective and functional design for future pedestrian, foot and shared paths and to enhance existing pathways with safety conditions.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: These shared paths are usually demarcated by a visual line between the pedestrian path and the path for cyclists.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We should also not forget that the existing shared paths are bi-directional.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, existing shared paths are only segregated between different users, that is, pedestrians and cyclists.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Not only does that mean that there is a narrower pathway for cyclists and riders of mobility vehicles, moving bi-directionally, they must also be mindful of other pedestrians also moving bi-directionally, using the same path.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Further, without a physical barrier that segregates pedestrians from other cyclists and riders of mobility vehicles, there is a tendency to stray into each other's lane, either because of personal convenience or in situations where the shared path is particularly crowded or when visibility is low at night.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I am sure many of us have encountered such situations or have ourselves been guilty of walking or cycling along paths not meant for such purposes.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Without physical segregated pathways for different kinds of users as well as segregation of pathways per direction, it is surely a recipe for accidents to occur.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: There are clearly safety risks we take when we try to shoehorn different and sometimes competing needs into the same design solution.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is largely for such reasons that countries like the Netherlands build separate pathways for cyclists and pedestrians.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, such segregated pathways might be able to accommodate higher volumes of users and, as such, it is a more efficient use of space than non-segregated shared paths.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, this Bill is a good opportunity for us to rethink our urban and estate planning and redesign our existing paths so that we can achieve a culture shift in our mobility choice with the assurance of safety and transport efficacy.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Just one last point on the issue of design.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that the Ministry is looking at reinforcing existing pathways to ensure that the surfaces of such pathways would better cushion against the impact of a fall.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I also hope that the Minister can shed some light on what is being done to enhance existing pedestrian, foot and shared paths to ensure the path is safe for all users, as well as how the Government ensures the regular maintenance, proper illumination and repair works of these paths.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I now turn to the issue of conflict management.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Conflicts are but a natural consequence of human interaction.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: What I am concerned about is how we seek to resolve such disputes that arise from the shared use of these paths which affect people from all walks of life.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: If the offender is prosecuted and convicted in criminal Court, the Court will consider if compensation to the victim should be paid."
